# PBMC 3k — Data Description

Source: 10x Genomics 3k PBMCs, via `scanpy.datasets.pbmc3k()`.
Modality: **tabular** (single-cell RNA-seq count matrix).

## Contents of prepared.npz
- `X`: (2638, 16579) raw UMI counts (cells x genes), float32.
  NOT normalized, NOT log-transformed, NOT gene-filtered beyond dropping
  genes detected in zero cells.
- `y`: cell-type annotation from scanpy's official PBMC3k tutorial
  (`sc.datasets.pbmc3k_processed()`, column `louvain`), matched by barcode.
  62 of 2700 cells had no label and were dropped.
  May be used as a conditioning variable when the objective needs
  class-specific generation; it is a community annotation, not a perfect
  ground truth.
- `split`: fixed stratified split (75% train / 25% test,
  seed 774). Fit preprocessing and generative models on `train` ONLY;
  `test` is the untouched real reference for evaluation.
- `feature_names`: gene symbols. `sample_ids`: cell barcodes.

## Class counts
  - CD4 T cells: 1144 total (858 train / 286 test)
  - CD14+ Monocytes: 480 total (360 train / 120 test)
  - B cells: 342 total (256 train / 86 test)
  - CD8 T cells: 316 total (237 train / 79 test)
  - NK cells: 154 total (115 train / 39 test)
  - FCGR3A+ Monocytes: 150 total (113 train / 37 test)
  - Dendritic cells: 37 total (28 train / 9 test)
  - Megakaryocytes: 15 total (11 train / 4 test)

## Things to confirm with inspect_data.py rather than assume
- Very sparse, highly skewed counts; library size varies between cells.
- Genes (p) far outnumber cells (n) — most genes are near-silent.
- Strong class imbalance; the rarest classes have only a handful of test cells,
  so per-class test metrics for them are noisy.

---
name: objective
description: Turn the user's objective into a task type, a success criterion and an evaluation plan — and decide whether generative modeling is warranted at all.
---

# When to apply
Right after inspecting the data, before any modeling decision.

# Step 1 — classify the objective

| Task type | Typical wording | What the generative model is FOR | How success is measured (evaluate.py) | Families that fit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Synthetic data release / data sharing | "share instead of real data", "privacy", "synthetic dataset" | replace real data for others' analyses | fidelity + memorization + `utility --utility tstr` | conditional DDPM (images), cVAE (tabular), WGAN-GP if n is large |
| Class balancing | "rare classes", "under-represented", "rebalance" | add samples of chosen classes only | `utility --utility augment` (vs class-weighting / oversampling), per-class fidelity, label consistency | cVAE (small n), conditional DDPM (images, enough data) |
| Data augmentation (scarce data) | "small training set", "augment" | add realistic variety to a small real set | `utility --utility augment --real-max N` | as for balancing |
| Anomaly / OOD / QC screening | "flag unusual", "outliers", "quality control" | a density or typicality score for each real sample | `score.py` + `anomaly` (AUROC vs baselines) | flow (exact log p), VAE (ELBO) |
| Representation learning | "latent space", "embedding", "features" | an encoder z = f(x) | label consistency / downstream classifier on z (report qualitatively if no tool) | VAE (L14) |
| Imputation / denoising | "missing values", "reconstruct" | p(x_missing \| x_observed) | reconstruction error on held-out masked entries | VAE, DDPM (not supported by the current tools — say so) |
| Uncertainty quantification | "how confident", "how typical" | likelihoods / posterior spread | calibration of scores (qualitative here) | flow, VAE |

If an objective mixes types, name the primary one and evaluate that first.
If the requested task is not supported by the tools (e.g. imputation),
state it, do the closest supported analysis, and flag the gap in the report.

# Step 2 — decide whether to generate at all

Generative modeling is the WRONG first tool when:

- **The problem it would fix is not present.** Balancing a dataset whose
  class imbalance ratio (`profile.json → labels.imbalance_ratio_max_over_min`)
  is below ~3 rarely helps; say so and show the evidence (class counts, and
  optionally a `real_only` vs `real_class_weighted` comparison).
- **A cheap non-generative fix exists and has not been tried.** For class
  imbalance: class weights and random oversampling. These are ALWAYS the
  baselines; synthetic data must beat them to be recommended.
- **There is too little data to learn a distribution.** With ~10 training
  samples in a class, any "generated" sample is an interpolation of those
  few samples. That can still be useful for balancing, but must be described
  honestly (it adds smoothness, not new information).
- **The objective needs real-world evidence**, e.g. evaluating a
  classifier. Test sets must stay real; synthetic data never replaces them.

Declining is a complete, valid outcome: log the decision with the numbers
that justify it, run the cheap supporting evidence, and write the report.
If you decide to generate anyway in a borderline case, say why.

# Step 3 — write down the success criterion BEFORE training
Log it as the `objective` decision. Make it concrete and falsifiable, e.g.

- balancing: "recommend synthetic augmentation only if macro-F1 of
  real+synthetic beats the BEST non-generative baseline and the paired
  bootstrap CI of the difference excludes 0; otherwise recommend the baseline";
- release: "TSTR accuracy ≥ ~0.8× train-on-real at equal size, C2ST clearly
  below 1.0, and no sign of copying (`frac_nearest_real_is_train` close to
  its expected value)";
- anomaly: "AUROC well above 0.5 AND above the trivial baselines reported
  next to it (PCA reconstruction error, image complexity alone)".

Also decide what "the real reference" is (which classes, which split) and
whether labels are needed for conditioning.

---
name: preprocessing
description: Choose the --prep spec, i.e. the space in which the generative model is trained and in which synthetic samples will live.
---

# When to apply
After interpreting the objective, before choosing the model family (the two
interact — re-check this once the family is known).

# Key idea
The generative model learns the distribution of the PREPROCESSED data. The
synthetic samples therefore live in that "model space" (e.g. log-normalized
expression of 2,000 genes), not in the raw format. Choose the space the
downstream user actually needs, and state it in the recommendation.

# Available steps (`tools/common.py::Prep`; comma-separated, applied in order)
`libnorm[:T]`, `log1p`, `hvg:N`, `standardize`, `pca:K`, `scale01`,
`scale_pm1`, `none`. All statistics are fit on the train split.

# Tabular / count data (e.g. single-cell RNA-seq)
Evidence to check in `profile.json`: `integer_valued`, `fraction_zeros`,
`row_sum.max_over_min`, `skewness_median_feature`,
`variance_share_top{N}_features`, `after_log1p_variance_share_top2000`,
`samples_per_feature`.

- Integer counts with very different row sums (max/min ≫ 1) → `libnorm`
  first, otherwise the model mostly learns sequencing depth.
- Heavy right skew → `log1p` (the Gaussian decoders/noise used by every
  family here assume roughly symmetric features).
- Many more features than samples (`samples_per_feature` ≪ 1) → reduce:
  `hvg:N` keeps interpretable features (N ≈ 1,000–3,000 for scRNA-seq;
  check how much log-variance the top N retain). Add `pca:K` (K ≈ 30–50)
  when the family needs a low dimension relative to n — normalizing flows
  and GANs on small n.
- `standardize` puts features on one scale (helps optimization; with a
  learned per-feature variance in the VAE it is optional). Synthetic values
  are then in z-score units — say so.

# Images
- DDPM / WGAN with conv backbone: `scale_pm1` (output layer uses tanh;
  DDPM clips its x0 prediction to [-1, 1]).
- Conv normalizing flow: `scale01` is REQUIRED (the flow models 8-bit
  pixels with dequantization; likelihoods are then in bits/dim).
- VAE conv: `scale01` or `scale_pm1` both work.
- Do not flatten images for conv models; use `--backbone conv`. Use `mlp`
  on images only for a deliberately cheap baseline.

# Subsampling (`--max-train`)
A compute decision, not a preprocessing one, but log it here too: when n
is large relative to the budget, a stratified subsample (e.g. 10k–30k
images) usually costs little quality. Never subsample the rare classes you
are trying to model — `--max-train` is stratified, but check
`run_config.json → train_class_counts`.
---
name: model-selection
description: Choose the generative model family (VAE, WGAN-GP, normalizing flow, DDPM), whether to condition on labels, and the backbone — by comparing the families against this dataset and objective.
---

# When to apply
After the objective and preprocessing decisions. Then read the chosen
family's own skill (`vae`, `gan`, `flow`, `diffusion`) to configure it.

# The four families side by side (lectures L14–L17)

| | VAE (L14) | WGAN-GP (L15) | Normalizing flow (L16) | DDPM (L17) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Per-sample likelihood | lower bound (ELBO) | none | **exact** log p(x) | none here |
| Sample quality (images) | blurry (decoder mean) | sharp when it works | usually weak | **best** |
| Data needed | **small n OK** (hundreds) | large (≥ ~10k) | moderate; low D for tabular | large (≥ ~5–10k) |
| Training stability | **stable** | fragile (mode collapse, balance) | stable, but D×layers memory | stable, slow to converge |
| Compute (train / sample) | cheap / cheap | moderate / cheap | moderate / cheap | **expensive / expensive** (many denoising steps) |
| Latent representation | **yes** (encoder q(z\|x)) | no encoder | invertible z, same dim as x | no compact latent |
| Class conditioning | easy | easy | easy | easy (+ classifier-free guidance) |

# Decision rules (apply in order, log which one decided)

1. **Objective needs a likelihood / typicality score** (anomaly, QC, OOD,
   uncertainty) → **flow** (exact) as primary; VAE ELBO is a reasonable
   alternative/baseline. GAN and DDPM are out (no per-sample likelihood in
   these tools).
2. **Objective needs a latent representation** → **VAE**.
3. **Objective needs samples** (release, balancing, augmentation):
   - **Small n** (hundreds to a few thousand rows, or a target class with
     only tens of training samples) → **conditional VAE**. DDPMs and GANs
     overfit or fail to converge at this size.
   - **Images with enough data** (≥ ~5k training images) and quality
     matters → **conditional DDPM**. Consider a conditional VAE as the cheap
     baseline only if the comparison is informative for the report.
   - **Large tabular data** → cVAE first; WGAN-GP or tabular DDPM are
     alternatives when cVAE samples are too smooth (low recall) and there is
     budget.
   - Choose WGAN-GP over DDPM only for a specific reason (e.g. sampling
     speed is a hard requirement). Its failure modes need extra checks.
4. **Budget check.** Estimate cost before committing: run a 1-epoch probe
   (`--epochs 1 --max-minutes 1`) and read `seconds` in `train_log.json`.
   If the chosen family cannot reach a useful number of updates inside the
   budget (DDPM: ≥ ~10k optimizer steps on 28×28 images), shrink it
   (subsample, smaller `ch`) or fall back to the cheaper family — and log it.

# Conditioning
- Use `--conditional` whenever the objective needs control over which
  class is generated (balancing, labeled release). Unconditional is fine
  for anomaly scoring of "normal" data (train only on the normal classes
  with `--include-classes` / `--exclude-classes`).
- With a very rare class (≈10 training samples), a conditional model may
  not learn the label well. Plan to check label consistency after
  sampling (evaluation skill), and see the VAE skill for posterior-based
  sampling.

# Backbone
- Images → `conv` (spatial structure; neighbour-pixel correlation in
  `profile.json` is typically ≥ 0.8).
- Tabular → `mlp`.

# How many models?
One primary model, plus at most one alternative when the comparison
answers a question the report needs (e.g. "is the expensive DDPM worth it
over a cVAE?"). Running every family is NOT the goal — the instructions
reward justified choices, not exhaustive benchmarks.
---
name: vae
description: Configure, train, check and sample a (conditional) VAE with tools/train.py --model vae.
---

# Model (tools/models/vae.py)
Encoder q(z|x[,y]) → Gaussian latent; decoder p(x|z[,y]) Gaussian with a
learned per-feature variance, so the ELBO is a real lower bound on log p(x)
(usable by `score.py`). Loss = −ELBO with a β weight on the KL term and a
linear KL warm-up.

# Hyperparameters (`--params` JSON) — starting points
| param | tabular (n ≈ 10³) | images 28×28 |
|---|---|---|
| `latent_dim` | 8–16 (≈ number of biological axes; more for more classes) | 16–32 |
| `hidden` (mlp) | [512, 256] | — |
| `ch` (conv) | — | 32 |
| `beta` | 1.0 (lower, e.g. 0.5, if samples are too smooth) | 1.0 |
| `kl_warmup_epochs` | 10–20 | 3–5 |
Other: `--lr 1e-3`, `--batch-size 64–128`; epochs: tabular 100–300 (fast);
images 10–30 on a subsample.

# Health checks (train_log.json → final_diagnostics)
- `posterior_collapse_suspected` / `active_units`: if 0 active units or KL
  ≈ 0, the decoder ignores z → lower `beta`, lengthen warm-up, or shrink
  the decoder.
- `kl_per_latent_dim`: a few dims near 0 is normal (unused capacity).
- Loss curve flattening = converged; still falling at the end = could
  train longer if budget allows.

# Sampling (tools/sample.py)
- Default: z ~ p(z) = N(0, I), decoded with the decoder MEAN. Means are
  smoother than real data: expect high precision, low recall. For tabular
  data `--add-noise` also draws the observation noise (wider spread; check
  that precision does not collapse).
- **Rare classes: check label consistency.** If a conditional VAE's
  prior samples for a class are classified as that class much less often
  than real data is (`metrics → fidelity.label_consistency.per_class`), the
  class's latent region does not line up with the prior — typical when it
  has only tens of training samples. Re-sample with
  `--latent-source posterior` (z ~ q(z|x) of random real training samples
  of that class) or `--latent-source interpolate` (random interpolations of
  two same-class training latents), and log it as an `iteration`.
  These are anchored to real training samples by construction: they will
  sit closer to training data (memorization metrics will show it). That is
  acceptable for balancing/augmentation; it is NOT acceptable for a
  privacy-motivated release.
- `--temperature` < 1 trades diversity for typicality.

# Typical outputs to report
loss curve, active units / KL, label consistency per class, precision vs
recall, and which latent source was used.

|---|---|---|---|---|

  privacy-motivated release.

recall, and which latent source was used.

---
name: evaluation
description: Choose which evaluate.py tasks measure the objective, and interpret every metric relative to its real-vs-real reference.
---

# When to apply
After sampling (or scoring), before deciding whether to iterate, and
again when writing the evaluation section.

# Pick tasks from the objective
| Objective | `--tasks` | extra flags |
|---|---|---|
| synthetic release | `fidelity,memorization,utility` | `--utility tstr` |
| class balancing | `fidelity,memorization,utility` | `--utility augment` (samples of the rare classes only) |
| augmentation for scarce data | `fidelity,utility` | `--utility augment --real-max N` |
| anomaly / QC | `anomaly` (after `score.py`) | `--anomaly-classes ...` |
Run fidelity on every sample set you plan to recommend.

# Golden rule: never read a metric alone
Every fidelity metric comes with `reference_real_train_vs_real_test`: the
same metric computed between two REAL samples. That is the best achievable
value at this sample size. Report both and judge the gap.
With class-specific samples, the real reference is automatically
restricted to the generated classes (`real_reference_classes`).

# Fidelity (feature space: `feature_space` in metrics.json)
- **precision** = fraction of synthetic samples that land in the real
  data's region → *realism*. **recall** = fraction of real samples covered
  by the synthetic data's region → *diversity / coverage*. Typical
  patterns: VAE decoder means → high precision, low recall; mode collapse
  → low recall; noisy samples → low precision. k-NN recall is inflated when
  the synthetic set is much smaller than the real set — compare at similar
  sizes.
- **frechet** (FID-style): 0 = identical Gaussian summaries. Use the RATIO
  to the reference. Ignore it when `frechet_unreliable_small_n` is true.
- **mmd_rbf**: ≈ 0 when distributions match; compare to the reference.
- **c2st_accuracy** (classifier two-sample test): 0.5 = indistinguishable;
  ~0.5–0.6 hard to tell apart; > ~0.9 easily distinguishable. The
  reference is ≈ 0.5 by construction; anything far above is a real gap.
- **label_consistency** (conditional samples): a classifier trained on real
  data predicts the intended label of synthetic samples. Compare
  `accuracy_on_synthetic` with `reference_accuracy_on_real_test` and check
  `per_class` — a low value for one class means the model did not learn
  that class (common for very rare classes; see VAE skill).
- **embedding.png**: real vs synthetic in a shared PCA — look for missing
  classes or clusters.

# Memorization
- `frac_nearest_real_is_train` vs `..._expected_if_no_memorization`
  (≈ 0.5): for each synthetic sample, is its nearest real neighbour a
  training sample or a held-out test sample (equal-sized pools)? Near the
  expected value → no sign of copying. ≥ ~0.7 → samples hug training data.
  Interpret against the sampling mode: posterior/interpolated VAE samples
  are anchored to training samples by design.
- `n_exact_copies` > 0 is a red flag for any data release.
- `ratio_synthetic_over_real` < 1 alone can just mean the samples are
  smoother (decoder means) — use it together with the membership fraction.

# Utility
- **tstr**: `train_on_synthetic` vs `train_on_real_same_size` on the real
  test set; `tstr_over_trtr_accuracy` ≥ ~0.8 is good for small models;
  `macro_f1_diff_95ci` shows if the gap is significant.
- **augment**: compare `real_plus_synthetic` against ALL three baselines
  (`real_only`, `real_class_weighted`, `real_random_oversample`), using
  `macro_f1`, `focus_classes_mean_f1` and `per_class_f1`. Use the paired
  bootstrap CIs in `macro_f1_diff_95ci`: if the CI vs the best baseline
  includes 0, there is NO demonstrated benefit. Check
  `n_test_per_focus_class`: with < ~10 test samples per class, per-class
  numbers are anecdotal — say so.

# Anomaly
- `auroc` (0.5 = chance) and `auprc` vs `auprc_chance`.
- Always compare with `baseline_pca_recon_error_auroc` and, for images,
  `complexity_check` (see flow skill). A model that does not beat trivial
  baselines is not useful as-is.
- `mean_logp_per_dim_by_class`: which classes the model finds typical.

# When to iterate (max three times, log each)
- label consistency low for the target classes → change sampling (VAE
  latent source, DDPM guidance);
- recall very low with high precision → more diversity: VAE
  `--temperature` > 1 (e.g. 1.5–2 with posterior sampling) and/or
  `--add-noise`; DDPM lower guidance; retrain with lower β. Check that
  label consistency stays high when diversity goes up;
- training health check failed → fix per the family skill;
- anomaly AUROC ≤ complexity baseline → report the corrected score or try
  the VAE ELBO.
Stop when the success criterion is met, the budget is spent, or the
remaining options are unlikely to change the recommendation.
---
name: recommendation
description: Turn the evaluation into a concrete, honest recommendation for downstream use of the generated data (or of the model's scores).
---

# When to apply
After evaluation, before writing the report. Log the result as the
`recommendation` decision.

# Structure every recommendation as
1. **Verdict** — one of: *Use* · *Use with restrictions* · *Do not use
   (use <alternative> instead)*.
2. **For what, exactly** — the specific downstream task, and the files to
   use (e.g. `outputs/<run>/<label>/samples_<tag>.npz`, which classes,
   how many).
3. **Evidence** — the 2–3 metrics that decided it, each with its reference
   or baseline.
4. **Restrictions and caveats** — see the checklist below.
5. **What would change the verdict** — e.g. more training time, more real
   samples of a class, a different score.

# Decision guide by objective

**Class balancing / augmentation**
- *Use* only if real+synthetic beats the best non-generative baseline
  with a CI excluding 0 (or a clear, consistent gain on the focus classes
  when test counts are too small for a CI to be informative — say so).
- If not: recommend the best simple baseline (class weights or
  oversampling) and explain that the synthetic data showed no measurable
  benefit. That is a useful result, not a failure.
- If the samples were generated around real training samples (VAE
  posterior/interpolation), describe them as "smoothed variations of the
  N real cells", not as new biology.

**Synthetic data release**
- *Use for prototyping / method development* if TSTR is reasonably close
  to train-on-real, label consistency is high and there is no sign of
  copying.
- Never for final model evaluation or scientific claims about the real
  population; never replace the real test set.
- Any memorization flag → *Do not release* until fixed; this overrides
  good fidelity.

**Anomaly / QC screening**
- Recommend the score that performed best *including* trivial baselines
  (e.g. the complexity-corrected likelihood if it beats the raw one).
- Use as a triage tool that flags samples for human review, with a
  threshold chosen on validation data for the acceptable false-positive
  rate — not as automatic exclusion.
- Name which classes it catches and which it misses
  (`mean_logp_per_dim_by_class`).

# Caveat checklist (include all that apply)
- The space the samples live in (e.g. "log-normalized, standardized
  expression of 2,000 HVGs" — not raw counts, not other genes).
- Synthetic rows must be marked as synthetic in any downstream table.
- Evaluation and test data stay real.
- Small-sample warnings (rare classes with very few real test samples).
- Budget limits (training stopped by time limit; quality could improve).
- Label noise: synthetic labels are only as good as label consistency.
- Patient privacy: no formal privacy guarantee (no differential privacy);
  memorization checks are evidence, not proof.

  expression of 2,000 HVGs" — not raw counts, not other genes).
- Synthetic rows must be marked as synthetic in any downstream table.
- Evaluation and test data stay real.
- Small-sample warnings (rare classes with very few real test samples).
- Budget limits (training stopped by time limit; quality could improve).
- Label noise: synthetic labels are only as good as label consistency.
- Patient privacy: no formal privacy guarantee (no differential privacy);
  memorization checks are evidence, not proof.
usage: evaluate.py [-h] --run RUN [--tasks TASKS] [--samples-tag SAMPLES_TAG]
                   [--utility {tstr,augment}] [--real-max REAL_MAX]
                   [--anomaly-classes ANOMALY_CLASSES]
                   [--clf-epochs CLF_EPOCHS] [--data DATA] [--device DEVICE]
                   [--seed SEED]

evaluate.py — evaluate generated data (and/or likelihood scores) for a run.

  python tools/evaluate.py --run outputs/r2/ddpm --tasks fidelity,memorization,utility --utility tstr
  python tools/evaluate.py --run outputs/r1/cvae --tasks fidelity,memorization,utility          --utility augment --samples-tag balance
  python tools/evaluate.py --run outputs/r3/flow --tasks anomaly --anomaly-classes background,debris

Every metric is reported next to a REAL-vs-REAL reference value computed the
same way (e.g. real-train vs real-test), because absolute numbers mean little
on their own. The script computes; it does not judge — interpretation
thresholds live in .agents/skills/evaluation/SKILL.md.

Tasks
  fidelity      Frechet distance, k-NN precision/recall (Kynkaanniemi et al. 2019),
                RBF-MMD, classifier two-sample test (C2ST), label consistency
                (does a real-trained classifier agree with the synthetic labels?),
                per-class precision/recall, 2-D PCA picture of real vs synthetic.
  memorization  distance from each synthetic sample to its nearest TRAIN sample,
                compared with the same distance for held-out real TEST samples.
  utility       --utility tstr    : train-on-synthetic / test-on-real vs train-on-real
                --utility augment : real train + synthetic vs real only, class
                                    re-weighting and random oversampling baselines
  anomaly       AUROC / AUPRC of -log p from score.py (needs scores_test.npz), a PCA
                reconstruction-error baseline, and (images) a check of whether the
                likelihood just tracks image complexity.

Feature space used for comparisons
  tabular: model space (after the run's preprocessing) projected to <=50 PCs fit on real train
  image  : 128-d penultimate features of a small CNN trained once on real train
           (cached in outputs/_cache/<dataset>/), a domain-specific stand-in for the
           Inception network used by FID.

head='''# generated_report_1: PBMC 3k — synthetic cells to rebalance rare cell types
**Verdict:** Synthetic cells from a conditional VAE did not improve cell-type classification of the rare types beyond simple class weighting, so they are not recommended.

## 1. Summary
- **Question:** Can synthetic megakaryocytes and dendritic cells improve a classifier on rare cell types?
- **Approach:** A conditional variational autoencoder (VAE) trained on 1,978 training cells; 200 synthetic cells for each of the two rarest types were added to a logistic-regression classifier and compared with three simple fixes.
- **Result:** Overall accuracy (macro-F1) was 0.903 with synthetic cells versus 0.908 on real data alone; all confidence intervals include 0.
- **Recommendation:** Use class weighting (or real data alone); do not use the synthetic cells.

## 2. Data at a glance
- 2,638 cells × 16,579 genes, raw counts, 95% zeros; cell depth varies 16-fold.
- Eight cell types; imbalance is 76-fold (CD4 T cells 858 training cells vs megakaryocytes 11, dendritic cells 28).
- The held-out test set has only 4 megakaryocytes and 9 dendritic cells, so rare-type scores are anecdotal.
- Genes far outnumber cells (0.16 cells per gene), so the model works on 2,000 highly variable genes (depth-normalised, log-transformed, standardised).

![Data profile](../$o/profile.png)

## 3. Decision path
'''+r("decision_path.md")+'''
The turning point was the first sampling attempt: cells drawn from the model's prior were recognised as the intended type only 7% of the time, so sampling was redone around real rare cells, which fixed label agreement but not the downstream benefit.

## 4. What was generated
400 synthetic cells (200 megakaryocytes, 200 dendritic cells) in the 2,000-gene standardised log-expression space. They are decoded from the latent codes of random real training cells of that type, with extra spread. They are therefore smoothed variants of 11 and 28 real cells, not new biology.
